scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Ten original B1 questions on Lara's learning habits: beliefs, reasoning and new situations. This is a teacher-review draft, NOT an approved school test.

tabs.title: Understanding Lara
tabs.description: Understand her thoughts and how she approaches a problem.

tabs.title: Reasons and Changes
tabs.description: Explain why events matter and how her thinking changes.

tabs.title: Using the Lesson
tabs.description: Choose sensible ways to use the ideas in everyday situations.

questions.q: What did Lara believe when she could not do something well at once?
choices: A teacher should always explain the task in a different way.
Trying a new subject was usually more enjoyable.
She might not have enough natural ability for it.
She needed to spend more time reviewing easy subjects.
questions.explanation: Paragraph one says that Lara took a difficult first attempt as a sign that she was not talented enough.

questions.q: Why might playing in front of the class have felt especially difficult for Lara?
choices: She had practised too long without taking a break.
Making visible mistakes challenged how she wanted others to see her.
She preferred to practise whole pieces rather than difficult sections.
She believed the teacher had already praised her performance.
questions.explanation: The public mistakes conflict with Lara's earlier fear that other pupils would notice what she could not do.

questions.q: What does Lara's practice over several days suggest about making progress?
choices: It mainly depends on working as quickly as possible.
It works best when a learner changes tasks every day.
It becomes easier when mistakes are no longer noticed.
It may take several short attempts rather than one long try.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph shows Lara practising a few minutes each day rather than endlessly repeating the whole piece.

questions.q: Why does the writer say Lara did not become 'a brilliant musician'?
choices: The success mattered more for her attitude towards difficulties than for her talent.
She had not learnt to play the whole piece without stopping.
The teacher had asked her to learn only part of the music.
Her performance had become worse during the week.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph contrasts improved playing with a more important change in Lara's approach to mistakes.

questions.q: What is different about Lara's new question, 'What could I do differently?'
choices: It asks other people to decide whether she is talented.
It helps her find a reason to avoid a difficult subject.
It encourages her to think about a change she can try.
It shows that she no longer cares about her school marks.
questions.explanation: The new question looks for a practical action rather than a fixed judgement about Lara's ability.

questions.q: Why is checking the first wrong step in maths a sensible next move?
choices: It helps Lara find the part of the problem she needs to understand.
It means she no longer has to check any other part of the calculation.
It allows her to reach an answer without doing the full problem.
It proves that her earlier method of practising music was wrong.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three describes identifying where a calculation first went wrong instead of repeating everything.

questions.q: A student is nervous about speaking English because they may make mistakes. What could they learn from Lara?
choices: It is better to stay quiet until speaking feels completely easy.
Practising one difficult part and asking questions can be useful.
Students should work only on subjects where they get good marks.
It is important to speak quickly so others do not notice mistakes.
questions.explanation: Lara's experience suggests working on a manageable difficulty and no longer treating questions as a sign of failure.

questions.q: Why does Lara tell a younger pupil about her uncomfortable first attempt?
choices: To show that music lessons give better results than maths lessons.
To recommend choosing easier tasks whenever mistakes appear.
To explain that high marks are no longer important to her.
To show that a difficult start can lead to a better next attempt.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph shows Lara sharing a realistic lesson: careful practice helped without promising quick success.

questions.q: A classmate keeps getting one part of a presentation wrong but can do the rest well. What might Lara suggest?
choices: Start again from the beginning each time without changing the method.
Work on that difficult part separately, then try the full talk again.
Skip the difficult part because other parts are already good.
Choose a new presentation topic instead of practising this one.
questions.explanation: The classroom scenario transfers the strategy of concentrating on four difficult bars to a new type of task.

questions.q: What can we conclude from Lara's refusal to promise quick success?
choices: Learning a new skill is mostly a matter of natural talent.
The best method always produces high marks in one week.
Younger students need more help than older students.
A useful strategy can help even when improvement is slow.
questions.explanation: Lara says careful practice made the next attempt easier while refusing to promise a quick result.

sourceTitle: The Problem with Being Good at Everything
